name: Southwest Couloir

pitch_detail.notes: Broad couloir, easy scrambling on snow or the 'black stairs' rock band
Steepens near the notch between the summit and West Tower
Through Black Tooth Notch, then a traverse across the upper Northeast Face and an exposed final scramble to the true summit

rappel_detail.pull: A single 60m rope does every station on this descent; a 70m is not required. Roughly 30m rappels.
rappel_detail.notes: First rappel from the summit ridge, running close to straight down the ridgeline toward Black Tooth Notch.
rappel_detail.anchor: natural/fixed sling on horn or block
hazards: this rappel is the one repeatedly named for pulling rock down onto the person below
a doubled 50m rope will not reach the next station
rappel_detail.station: Reached by downclimbing roughly 100 ft from the summit to the first slings. These are the same anchors you climb past on the final pitches up and right — note where they are on the ascent, because they are much harder to spot on the way down.

rappel_detail.pull: Extending the rings out from the anchor is specifically recommended here to keep the pull clean.
rappel_detail.notes: Second rappel, notably traversing (trending skier's right/rappeller's left).
hazards: the sideways line offers the rope many places to catch and is the station most often named in stuck-rope accounts
enough swing that parties describe hooking a horn on the way across to stop the pendulum
rappel_detail.station: Distinctly traversing, trending skier's right and rappeller's left rather than down the fall line.

rappel_detail.notes: Third rappel, also traversing, reaching Black Tooth Notch; from there scramble/simul-climb an exposed 4th-class connecting ledge.
hazards: the last few feet often need to be scrambled off rappel; setting an intermediate anchor is optional
the connecting ledge to the notch is a short loose Class 4 to low-5th traverse with one exposed move, usually simul-climbed or short-roped
the rope pulls with real drag off the slab at the bottom of this one
rappel_detail.station: The second traversing rappel, ending on or just above the long sidewalk ledge that leads around to Black Tooth Notch. A cairn marks the notch and can be seen on the way up, so note its position before you need it.

rappel_detail.notes: First of three further rappels down into the Southwest Couloir.
hazards: the next station is out of sight from this one; accounts disagree on whether it lies on a hidden ledge to rappeller's left or straight down at the very end of a 60m rope, so be ready for either before you commit
some parties skip this station and scramble about 15 m down to the next
rappel_detail.station: Ten to thirty feet down the southwest side of the notch on fixed slings, at the top of the Southwest Couloir. From here the line runs down the fall line, so you are hunting tat rather than a landmark.

hazards: the rock through the couloir is thoroughly loose and the second person down is directly beneath whatever the first dislodges
a 60m rope is just barely long enough on one of the raps in this section
rappel_detail.station: Straight down the couloir on fixed slings.

rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel into the Southwest Couloir, from which the descent continues toward North Fork Bridge Creek.
hazards: the couloir ends in cliffs and a waterfall band below; exit left onto easier terrain and traverse back into the basin rather than following the fall line, which cliffs out
the exit ledges are crumbly, and there is still several thousand feet of off-trail ground below before the valley — parties get benighted on it
rappel_detail.station: The final rappel takes you off technical rock into the open couloir, landing on Class 3 ground or snow depending on season.

rappels: 6 single-rope rappels on a 60 m rope: 3 from the summit to Black Tooth Notch (the second and third traversing), then 3 straight down the fall line into the Southwest Couloir; below that, scramble and downclimb the couloir
descent_text: Descend the same Southwest Couloir used on ascent, after rappelling into it from the summit. From the summit area, downclimb broad class 3-4 terrain in the couloir, staying alert for a band of more solid darker rock on the left side (locally called the 'black stairs') which offers cleaner downclimbing than the surrounding rotten rock; the couloir is otherwise loose and rockfall-prone, so groups should descend close together or one at a time through narrows. Lower down, if snow still fills the gully (common into mid-summer), this is a fast plunge-step or glissade; late-season parties will instead pick through talus and scree for several hundred feet. The couloir's mouth opens onto cliffy ground above a waterfall, so exit left (climber's left) onto easier heather benches rather than continuing straight down into the cliffs — this is the one real route-finding crux of the descent. Below that, drop into heather meadows around 7,700 ft where running water is usually found, then retrace the approach line back down through the brush and along the North Fork Bridge Creek Trail and PCT to the Bridge Creek trailhead. The top of the descent is a rappel line, not a downclimb: from the summit, three single-rope rappels reach Black Tooth Notch, and three more drop straight down the fall line into the couloir; a 60 m rope is enough. Below those, the couloir is the scramble and downclimb described above.
approach: From the Bridge Creek/PCT trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 159 (just over a mile east of Rainy Pass, ~4,400 ft), follow the Pacific Crest Trail southbound along Bridge Creek. This stretch loses elevation steadily — roughly 1,600 ft over about 9.5-9.6 miles — down through forest to the North Fork Camp junction, where the PCT crosses Bridge Creek (a footbridge here has been washed out in past years; check current NPS conditions before counting on it). At the junction, turn onto the North Fork Bridge Creek Trail and head upstream (north); this climber's/stock trail is roughly 7 miles long and regains about 1,700 ft, but grows progressively brushier and less maintained the farther up-valley you go, with alder and overgrowth becoming a real time sink in late summer. The trail eventually peters out in the big cirque below Goode, Storm King, and Mount Logan — most parties leave the maintained tread around mile 13-14 of the approach to ford the North Fork (a cold, sometimes knee-deep crossing; easier a short way upstream near a cairn) and pick up an intermittent boot path/cairns through talus and alder ('tunnel' sections of brush) toward the toe of the Goode Glacier. From there it's off-trail travel over moraine and glacier remnants (light crampons/axe useful if there's residual snow or open crevasses) to a rotten, blocky ridge that accesses the base of the couloir proper — expect loose, moving rock underfoot on this last stretch. Reasonable bivy options exist near the glacier toe (~6,400-6,800 ft, limited flat tent sites) or higher on ledges closer to the couloir base. Total approach is commonly done as a long day-plus-camp, on the order of 15-16 miles and 4,000-4,800 ft of gain to high camp; water is generally available at regular intervals along Bridge Creek and its tributaries but can be scarce higher up near camp, so fill up at the last reliable stream.
overview: The Southwest Couloir is the standard, least-technical route up Goode and the line of the 1936 first ascent. From the base, the route climbs a narrow couloir of snow, scree, and short rock steps, crosses through the Black Tooth Notch, then traverses across the upper Northeast Face before a short, exposed final section to the summit — even the 'easy' route on Goode involves real exposure near the top.
beta: From high camp, ascend to the saddle/notch and climb the steep, loose gully of the Southwest Couloir (class 4 at the top); a line of more solid darker rock on the left ('the black stairs') offers easier scrambling than the center of the gully.
gear: Crampons — often needed through the couloir well into midsummer
Light rock rack (small cams and nuts) — for the class 4 'black stairs' step and the summit ridge scramble above the couloir
Rope — some parties belay a horizontal slab pitch to reach the hidden exit gully rather than solo it
A few ice screws if climbing late season and the couloir has gone icy rather than snow
Helmet — loose rock in the couloir and on the black stairs
fa: Wolf Bauer, Philip Dickert, Joe Halwax, Jack Hossack, and George MacGowan, July 5, 1936 (original route to the peak's first ascent)
face: Southwest Couloir / Southeast Ridge, southwest side of Mt. Goode
